rules.plain_language_rule: Body composition refers to the relative contribution of tissues that make up body mass; for performance, fat mass and skeletal muscle are especially relevant.
Skeletal muscle contributes to force production and can support collision and movement performance.
Excess fat mass increases the mass that must be moved without directly contributing to force production.
Excess body fat may negatively affect acceleration, speed, endurance, and repeated work rate.
Body-composition requirements are position-specific; forwards and backs should not necessarily share identical targets.
Higher playing levels may combine greater total mass with lower relative fat mass.
Total body mass must always be interpreted alongside body composition.
Changes in body composition should be evaluated alongside changes in rugby-relevant performance.
The goal is optimal functional body composition, not maximum muscle mass or minimum body fat.
Body-composition targets must account for age, sex, maturation, position, playing level, and health.
Strength is the ability to produce force or resist unwanted movement.
Strength contributes to a wide range of rugby actions including tackling, scrummaging, mauling, lifting, sprinting, and evasion.
Strength development should therefore be a central component of rugby physical preparation.
Strength testing must be interpreted according to the mechanics of the test.
In bodyweight-plus-load exercises, total system mass may provide more meaningful information than external load alone.
Both absolute and relative strength can be relevant, depending on the player’s position and performance demands.
Strength should be assessed across relevant movement categories rather than represented by a single universal test.
Structured, progressive strength and conditioning pathways can produce meaningful physical-development advantages.
Development systems should be designed around available resources rather than assuming professional-level facilities are required.
The website should track strength longitudinally so progression, plateaus, and regressions can be identified.
